ON BIRD-CATCHING.

You will carry a dog’s tongue hidden in your shoe under your big toe, or if you carry a dried dog’s heart with you, according to Sextus; or hare’s hair or dung, according to Pliny. Or you will carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or you will give it a frog in a morsel of food; all these are for avoiding the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs flee the sight of anyone all day who expels a tick from a dog and carries it for a while. Oppian:

> *But if you carry a small piece of a hyena’s skin*
> *That has been cut off, immediately the puppies and fierce dogs*
> *Will be struck with bitter terror, and they will not bark at you*
> *As you walk by, even if they were barking before.*

### *So that a dog cannot run.*

If you smear its wings with oil, it will be hindered in its running; this will happen in this way.

### *So that a hawk may be spirited.*

You will animate the bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds; soak the food it uses during the hunting season in wine, or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into the beak of a dove chick, then make it fly. Thus:

### *You will make partridges more combative,*

If you give them sprigs of maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianti"</note> in their food, according to Pliny, and:

### *Roosters become more combative,*

By giving them garlic in their food when they are about to fight. From this, in an old comedy, they are most wittily called <term>ἐσκοροδισμένοι</term> <gloss>garlic-stuffed</gloss>, that is, fed with garlic, for one who is vehement and too prone to fighting.

### *So that a bird does not fly high,*

Pluck the tail feathers that direct its course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### *So that a bird cannot fly,*

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way, they do not escape in aviaries.

<summary>This page provides various folk remedies and practical techniques for managing animals, including methods to silence dogs, increase the aggression of hawks and roosters, and restrict the flight of birds.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page: Each one</meta> is distinguished by piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God, as if perceived by the eyes of true reason, and by the confidence of his own belief, standing out among men as much as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its divinity as by its holiness and divine nature. Believe, O Asclepius, that this is the second god, governing all things and illuminating all worldly living beings, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living being that always was, is, and will be, there is nothing mortal in the world. For in every living part that is within the world, just as in one and the same animal that is always living, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live always. Therefore, just as the world is eternal, so the sun is the eternal governor of vital things, or the frequent visitor and dispenser of all their vitality. Therefore, God is the eternal governor of the living, or of the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed it once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital things in the manner which I shall describe.

<summary>This passage identifies the sun as the second god and the eternal governor of all life within the world, emphasizing that the world and its living parts are inherently immortal and sustained by divine law.</summary>
<keywords>Asclepius, Sun, second god, eternal law, vitality, immortality, world-soul</keywords>

Varro testifies that he saw these. And there are things more wonderful than these: for on the Attic shore the sea sounds like a cithara. At Megara, a certain rock, when struck, produces the sound of a stringed instrument, so great is the power of Music. It itself soothes the soul, elevates the mind, incites combatants to war, and relieves the labors and fatigue of individual tasks. It recalls the fallen and the desperate, and comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by the singing of their guides. In a similar way, those carrying heavy burdens sing, and are enabled and lightened by it: for song produces delight and ability, mitigates the irascible, gladdens the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant, and dissipates vain thoughts: hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that some diseases of the body and mind can be cured or induced in this way. For the good is innate to truth, together with life and light, and no avenger <note>referring to the forces of darkness or vices</note> has approached to go beyond it. Indeed, all the avenging forces were cast out by a certain sudden impulse. You have understood, my son, the manner of regeneration itself. The intellectual generation is composed by the presence of the number ten, which rejects the number twelve. And we have contemplated this from the generation itself. Whoever, therefore, because of the kindness of the generation which is according to God, loses his bodily sense, knows himself to be composed of divine things, and having become unswerving, rejoices in the divine power with his whole mind. **TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the intuition of the eyes, but by the act of the mind, which is exercised through the inner powers. I am in heaven, in earth, in water, in air. I am in animals, in trees, in the body, before the body, and after the body. But I would have you tell me this besides: how are the avenging shadows repelled by the ten powers from the number twelve? What is the method, Trismegistus? **TRISM.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the zodiacal circle, which consists of that number twelve. And the numbers are eleven, and one which is omniform according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. Therefore, those avenging forces are in a way separated from one another, yet in acting they are in a way joined, as for example, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly, therefore, according to right reason, they are separated insofar as they are repelled by the ten powers, that is, by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the generator of the soul. Therefore, the gods are the princes of all species; these are followed by the gods whose prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence/substance</gloss>. These are sensible, of both origins, and similar to one another, who accomplish all things through sensible nature. Each one illuminates its own work through the other. Of the heavens, or whatever is comprehended by that name, the <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is Jupiter. For through the heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things. The <term>ousiarches</term> of the sun is light. For the good of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. Of the thirty-six stars fixed forever in the same place (whose name is <term>Horoscopij</term> <gloss>horoscopes/ascendants</gloss>), their <term>ousiarches</term> or prince is he whom they call <term>Pantomorphon</term> <gloss>all-formed</gloss> or Omniform. He who makes diverse forms for diverse species. The seven spheres which are called erratic have <term>ousiarchas</term> <gloss>rulers of essence</gloss>, that is, their own princes, whom they call Fortune, <term>eimarmenēs</term> <gloss>fate/destiny</gloss>, by which all things are changed, by the law of nature with most firm stability, and varied by eternal agitation. The air, indeed, is the organ, or machine of all things, through which all things are made. Moreover, the <term>ousiarches</term> of this is second. To mortals, mortal things; and to these, similar things. Therefore, with these things being so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are naturally connected in such a way that mortal things are annexed to mortals, and sensible things to sensibles. But the sum of governance obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, or rather, they are one. For all things depend from the one, and flow down from it rather; when they are distant, they are believed to be many, divided. But when united, they are one, or rather two: from whence all things are made, and by whom they are made. That is, from the matter of which they are made, and from his will, by whose nod other things are effected. ASCLEPIUS: This is again the reason, O Trismegistus. TRISMEGISTUS: Such it is, O Asclepius. For God, either as father or lord...

Indeed, arsenic certainly cannot be fixed at all, unless the operating artist has an equal knowledge of its coloring spirit, in which matter all philosophers have slumbered, vainly attempting to effect something from it. Whoever, therefore, is ignorant of this spirit should have no hope of fixing it, nor of attributing to it the virtue by which it might acquire the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening of which mention has been made is derived from a false foundation, and that by it copper is falsely whitened, not transmuted. Sophists, having masked and painted Venus <note>alchemical term for copper</note> in this manner, mixed it with double its weight of Luna <note>alchemical term for silver</note>, and sold it to goldsmiths and moneyers; in the end, however, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters, not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the sophists took red arsenic instead of white, and this too resulted in a false art. For in whatever way it is prepared, it exhibits nothing but whiteness. Some have proceeded further, to common sulfur, which they cooked with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urines for a day and a night, until it emerged white. Afterward, they elevated it from common salt and eggshells through sublimation, and cooked and sublimated it, and this many times; nevertheless, it remained always combustible, although white: yet, by this means, to fix raw mercury...

<summary>The author continues to debunk fraudulent alchemical practices, specifically criticizing the use of arsenic and sulfur to create a superficial "whitening" of copper, which he labels as the work of deceptive "sophists" rather than true philosophers.</summary>
<keywords>arsenic, Venus, copper, Luna, silver, sophists, counterfeiters, sulfur, sublimation, fixation</keywords>

where they should have taken <term>pyrites</term> <gloss>a metallic mineral</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials, they took instead substances in which there is no operation. From the workshops, these things are expensive, but in terms of labor, they are of no value at all. Our material, however, is not bought from any workshop; it is found daily in the streets, and merchants throw it away. It is sufficient, therefore, that it be found for free. But the material of our <term>stone</term> is compared to all those things with which the artisans labor. Indeed, our stone is our <term>salt</term>, our <term>mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, <term>saltpeter</term>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, and infinite other things of this kind, yet not dug from wild, rural mountains with hammers and other tools. Rather, our stone is extracted solely from our own mountains and fountains. In our <term>salt-fountain</term> our <term>salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>mercury</term>, and <term>sulphur</term> are poured, and not from wild, foreign, or rural mountains. The artisans do not understand these things, nor can they believe or comprehend them. For the Lord has obscured and closed their senses, and for this reason, they have used these things otherwise than they ought to have been used, and they have not hit the mark at all. Nevertheless, they have persisted in this contrary sense and have followed their own stubborn heads. For instance, when they should have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimed</term> with a strong fire; they scorched the <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>strong water/nitric acid</gloss>, and they immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. When they should have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> instead, and again, like those unskilled in the nature of things, they handled the matter ineptly. They fell into doubt and, with lying words, kept saying that the art was not true but false, in which, however, they rightly lie. For their own ignorance has shamefully deceived them, which must be imputed to their own obscure and murky cunning, while, according to their own dark intellect, they interpreted words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), those unskilled <term>Philosophasters</term> <gloss>pseudo-philosophers</gloss> understood it as burning, and they reduced the substances entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Likewise, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term>, or transmute into water, those <term>wiseacres</term> burned the nature with <term>aqua fortis</term>, and that same water, which has no power in

<meta>continues from previous page: ...the time of the fire requires, and the succession of its increase little by little, with caution, until it is fixed in its lime, so that it does not easily return into a body, so that a greater fire may be administered to it, for the perfection of its lime. Similarly, let him not happen to err in <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction, so that if at any time he places its lime into reduction, it happens to him that it does not reduce, but he finds it of the former disposition or reduced into glass, and he deems its reduction impossible. For we say that if he does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, however, he applies a great one, it does not necessarily happen that it reduces, but it is possible that it reduces it into vitrification <note>glass-like state</note>. And that is because <term>Jupiter</term> has a fugitive <term>argentum vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver/mercury</gloss> substance included in the depth of its nature. If it draws out a long delay in the fire, it will flee, and will leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be more apt to be converted to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. And therefore it is necessarily left that, with the most rapid impetus of fire, he hastens to reduce it quickly. Otherwise, it is not reduced. Therefore, let him practice at this, and he will know.

The second mode of calcination of these two bodies, <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> and <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown upon their surface, quantity after quantity very often in their fusion, and let it be mixed by much agitation through an iron rod, over the fire, until they are turned into ash through the mixture of salt. And afterwards, let their lime be perfected by the same mode of perfection, with its considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>plumbum</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> is converted to powder more easily from the first labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.

<summary>This page details the technical challenges of reducing tin and lead, specifically warning against the loss of internal mercury which leads to vitrification rather than metallic fusion, and describes a secondary method of calcination using salt.</summary>

829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a person, and from those highest parts their lower parts live and shine, and because Mohammed is present in their minds along with their religion, therefore some Mohammed is always placed in their view. And so that they may turn their faces toward the East, above which is the Lord, he is placed below the Christian center. It is not the Mohammed himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss>, but another who performs his office; nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Mohammedan. Because he had also been a Christian, he was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord, that He was not the son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Others have succeeded this Mohammed later. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like a torch, so that he may be recognized; but that fire is not visible to others, only to the Mohammedans.

830. The Mohammed himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss> does not come into view today. It was told to me that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as a god, he was cast out from his seat, which he had under the Papists, and sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mohammedans was stirred up by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God. So that the sedition might be quelled, Mohammed was brought up from the lower earth and shown, and then he was also seen by me. He appeared like those corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with a face tending toward black, and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to sink down.

831. Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith in three Divine Persons, and from that, the worship of three Gods, as many Creators; and furthermore, toward the Roman Catholics because of their genuflections before images. For this reason, they call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," and therefore that they divide Omnipotence and make three out of one and the One. They say they are like fauns with three horns, one for each god, and at the same time three for one, and that they pray in this way, chant in this way, and sound forth from their pulpits in this way.

832. The Mohammedans, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love what is just and do what is good from religion, have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one, they live honestly with several wives, but from there, no others are elevated into the higher Heaven except those who renounce concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This faith among them is the means by which ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mohammedan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved unless they were born a Christian. But the Mohammedan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these inquire where it is, and they also find it. It is in this: that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss> the book of their religion, and therefore Mohammed, who wrote it, has settled into their thoughts, and they follow him with some worship, they therefore think little about our Lord. So that it may be fully known that this religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be told in some order, but first concerning the origin of idolatries. ### On the images of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon. Chap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon, namely the figure of a serpent between an airy and a fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>Θ</gloss>. They made it when Jupiter held the mid-heaven with that head, which image they affirm contributes much to the success of petitions. They wished to signify by that image a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit</gloss>, and they wished to represent him through the image of a serpent. For the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all others, and celebrate its divine nature, because in it, above other animals, there exists a sharper and more ample spirit. This fact is shown both by its swift movement without any feet, hands, or other instruments, and because it repeatedly renews its age and becomes young again with extraordinary ease. They made an image of the tail in a similar way when the Moon was eclipsed in the tail, or was badly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made it for inducing anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil genius. A certain Hebrew had enclosed such an image in a golden, double belt, which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first of that name, King of Spain (whether knowingly or unknowingly). When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be surrounded by a serpent. Having subsequently discovered the magic power inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the mansions of the Moon. Chap. XLVI.

They also made images in the individual mansions of the Moon. In the first, for the destruction of someone, they made an image in an iron ring of a black man clothed in sackcloth and girded, throwing a lance with his right hand. They sealed it in black wax and fumigated it with liquid storax and uttered imprecations. In the second, against the anger of a prince and for his reconciliation, they sealed in white wax and mastic an image of a crowned king, and fumigated it with aloe wood. In the third, they made an image in a silver ring, the measure of which was square, and the figure of which was a woman well-dressed, sitting on a chair, with her right hand raised above her head. They sealed and fumigated it with musk, camphor, and aromatic nail <note>likely clove</note>. They asserted that this bestows prosperity of fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for vengeance and separation, enmity and malevolence, they sealed in red wax an image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and fumigated it with red myrrh and storax. In the fifth, for the favor of kings and officials and a good reception, they sealed from silver the head of a man, and fumigated it with sandalwood. In the sixth, for placing love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and fumigated it with aloe wood and amber. For God, as the Father of all, needs nothing; but it is good for us when we adore him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction from him. For instruction purges the mind, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward him. He indeed preached well about God the Father and said with what morals he should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the <term>Hebreorum</term> <gloss>Hebrews</gloss> are full of these precepts, whether the life of the saints is praised or blamed. But it was only among the Christians, or they are slandered as much as the demons—whom they think are gods—wish; as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in the theaters and temples for the sake of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to God, and from this to understand where there is a building up and where there is a ruin of morals. But who said this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and fitting lie, that Christians would rather revere than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we, in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love along with the celestial holy angels and the powers of God, whom we consider most blessed as citizens, forbids sacrificing in the law which he gave to his people, the Hebrews; and he threatened very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated." And lest anyone should think that it was commanded not to sacrifice to the worst demons and earthly spirits—whom this man calls mimes or lesser ones—because they were also called gods in the holy scriptures, not by the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but by the Gentiles, which the seventy interpreters clearly set down in the psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons," lest anyone should therefore think that while it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, it was permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones, or to all or some of them, he immediately added: "except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only. Lest perhaps someone, because he says "to the Lord alone," might think that there is only one God to whom one thinks one must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood in this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this philosopher gives such great testimony, gave a law to his own Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but already spread among all the Gentiles, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated, except to the Lord only." What need is there in this law of his and in his prophets to search for many things about this matter? Rather, there is no need to search, for they are not hidden or erased, but are open and frequent to collect, and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God wished to be sacrificed to by no one at all except to himself alone. Behold this one thing, briefly or rather grandly, menacingly, but truthfully said by that God whom their most learned men preach: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest eradication follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," he says, "shall be eradicated, except to the Lord only." Not because he needs anything, but because it is expedient for us that we be his. For to him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, you are my God, for you do not need my goods." But the most excellent and best sacrifice of this one is we ourselves. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have disputed in the preceding books. For the prophets of the Hebrews interpreted that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future were to cease, and that the Gentiles would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun even to its setting, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine argues that the God of the Hebrews, whom even pagan philosophers acknowledge, strictly forbids sacrifice to any but Himself. He clarifies that the prohibition against "gods" refers to demons, and that the true sacrifice is the life of the faithful, fulfilling the prophetic transition from Jewish ritual to the universal Christian offering.</summary>

The matter in which the **Lord** <note>original: "יה'וה"; the Tetragrammaton</note> **God** is recognized is that they are enacted through all the attributes that are completed by the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy. As you will find in the creation of the first man, and in his judgment, and in his expulsion, and in all those matters, you will find that they all came about through the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy. Everything is in complete perfection, with Mercy and Justice, all as is appropriate in true judgment. According to this principle, the Torah says: "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. The explanation of the verse is as follows: The Rock, who decrees judgment with strength, does not act with cruelty. He does not decree the judgment except that "His work is perfect," meaning that the judgment He decreed was previously consulted upon by the two attributes, Loving-kindness <note>Hebrew: *Chesed*</note> and Justice. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect," for the word "perfect" <note>Hebrew: *tamim*</note> is the secret of two things. It is as if it said "twins" <note>Hebrew: *te'umim*</note>, but in the language of honor, it speaks of the two things above using the word "perfect," and below using the word "twins." Thus it says: "And they shall be twins" <note>Exodus 26:24</note> below, "they shall be perfect" <note>Exodus 26:24</note> at the top. Below, they are twins; above, they are perfect. This is because below, they appear as two things, a thing and its opposite, like a helper and an accuser. But above, everything is one intention. Whether it is the helper or the accuser, both have one intention, and there is no hatred or love there, and no partiality, but only true judgment. Therefore, it says "His work is perfect," for He consulted in Justice and in Mercy and decreed the judgment, and this is the secret of true judgment. And what it says, "for all His ways are justice" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>, means everything is for the eye of every beholder, as it says, "for all His ways are justice." You already know that justice is included in Justice and in Mercy, for justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the middle line, who is the mediator between the two tents, which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Loving-kindness, Isaac corresponds to Justice, and Jacob decides between them, "a plain man, dwelling in tents" <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. And justice corresponds to Jacob, drawing from Loving-kindness on the side of Abraham and from Justice on the side of Isaac. Thus it says: "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have performed" <note>Psalm 99:4</note>. And the prophet said: "Correct me, O **Lord**, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing" <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The explanation of the verse is: "Correct me, O **Lord**, but with justice," what it says "but" <note>Hebrew: *akh*</note> divides, meaning in half the attribute of justice, which is Loving-kindness, for justice is half Justice and half Loving-kindness. Therefore, it says "but with justice," and then said "not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing," and revealed the secret to diminish half of the justice from the side of anger. Therefore, justice depends on Jacob, who is the father of the tribes. He knew great sorrow for his children when the Holy One, blessed be He, decreed upon them, so that he would seek mercy and righteousness for them. And the secret is: "And the **Lord** of Hosts is exalted in justice" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. What is written after it? "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. This means when the justice is exalted from the rest of the Justice and makes room for the attribute of **El** <note>God</note>, which is the secret of what is said, "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness." In total, when the **Lord** of Hosts is exalted in justice, the attribute of **El** comes, which is above, and performs righteousness, and the justice is worked. This is the secret of what they said, that justice is included in Loving-kindness and Justice, and it says: "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have performed." And the great secret is: "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne" <note>Psalm 89:15</note>, for righteousness is sometimes Justice, according to its reception of the abundance, as I explained that righteousness is great Justice in strength. But when justice participates with it, then the throne is established in Mercy. And if it is exalted in justice and reaches until Loving-kindness and Truth together, they are called the "shining faces," then everything is made into great Mercy, and this is the secret of "They shall precede"

### **Torah** Light. These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Service, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah is the commandment of "You shall not add and you shall not subtract," <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note> which points to the perfection of the Torah. It is as the philosophers said: a thing that is perfect in the ultimate sense, it is not appropriate to say it is lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it were capable of addition, it would be found not to be perfect. Therefore, the definition of the perfect is that it has neither lack nor excess. It is known that the Torah depends on His Great Name, which is <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>, the Torah of the Lord is perfect, as I have elaborated upon this in my tractate <term>Shevuot</term> <gloss>Oaths</gloss>, chapter "Torah Light." And as it is written in the <term>Zohar</term> <gloss>Book of Splendor</gloss> on this verse, "This is My name and this is My memorial." <note>Exodus 3:15</note> <term>Yod-He</term> with "My name" equals 365. <term>Vav-He</term> with "My memorial" equals 248. And it is written, "I am the first and I am the last." <note>Isaiah 44:6</note> And He is the absolute perfect; there is no diminution in Him nor addition. And regarding this comes the warning, "You shall not do so to the Lord your God," <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note> a warning against erasing the Name or smashing a stone from the Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are in the house in which He, may He be blessed, dwells; and likewise the Temple. And it is written, "I am the Lord, My name is..." The letters are like a closure for the house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul for them. And one who destroys His house, so to speak, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service refers to the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. And the commandment came to have a fixed place, and he came to the Chosen House and said a word with reason: "To His habitation you shall seek, and you shall come there." <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note> "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Yod-Vav</term>, as it is written, "And He descended upon Mount Sinai," and as it is written, "Do not fear, for it is I who will dwell," for in the Temple the Glory is unified in the splendor of His people. And this is "To His name, His name there," as the <term>Targum</term> <gloss>Aramaic translation</gloss> says, "To cause His <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> to dwell." And around the place of holiness, the wicked walk, for they are the <term>Kelipah</term> <gloss>husk/shell of impurity</gloss>. Therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in any place that you see." <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>

### **And sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them, to bring them inward. And this is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborns of the offering from outside the city to the Chosen House. And then the branch returns to its root, and it is written regarding them, "There you shall offer," <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note> meaning there they shall have an ascent, and not outside. And since in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, there is holiness, therefore we were commanded to be "turn from evil," to destroy all the places where the nations worshipped, and one must uproot and eradicate after them. And this we were commanded specifically in the Holy Land. And its secret is a hint to the ten nations, whose power is not that of idolaters. And the matter is that the nations who are in the Land of Israel under the rule of the Honored Name serve the Name by "cutting the shoots," <note>a metaphor for heresy or damaging the divine unity</note> and this is actual idolatry. However, those in the Diaspora are under the rule of the external forces. And just as there is a great prohibition to smash one stone from the holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eradicate an apostate city and not to rebuild it again, for its place is impure. And likewise, a seducer and enticer, to uproot and eradicate him, for he is from the impurity of the primordial serpent who was a seducer. And the Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the serpent," therefore the powers of the seducer do not recover. And the commandment came not to love him and not to listen to him, like the matter said regarding the serpent, "And I will put enmity between you and the woman." <note>Genesis 3:15</note> Also, a false prophet is like a seducer. Let us return to the matter, for the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. And this is the reason for the firstborns, that the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the firstborns, which are the first, point to great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, to a holy place they shall go, and from there they shall take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. And the secret of the lesser holy offerings and the second tithe is that their eating is in Jerusalem. And this is the grain, and the wine, and the oil, which are the fathers of the fathers of all sustenance. And it is forbidden to eat the lesser holy offerings until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul. And afterwards is the permission to enjoy. And know that just as the service, which is the offering, is an offering to the Lord, so is the one who serves, for the essence of the service is that he offers himself, in the secret of "When a man among you offers." <note>Leviticus 1:2</note> And the burnt offering is entirely consumed, for it comes upon the thought of "turn from evil," the thought which is spiritual, and he offers it all night, etc., the serpent does not hinder him. And the lesser holy offerings are the perfection of the soul and the body.

### **And the secret** of the firstborn is the secret of Israel, who are called holy, as it is written, "Israel is My firstborn." <note>Exodus 4:22</note> And He has compassion on them, "And you shall guard them," and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. And the secret of eating the holy offerings corresponds to the blemishes and defects in them. For Israel are holy, and Israel are called "man." And he was holy, afterwards a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," but he has a redemption, in the secret of "And I will give a man in your stead." <note>Isaiah 43:3</note> And this was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>the scapegoat</gloss>, "And it shall bear their iniquities." And the meaning is that they fall upon his head and upon his people. But we were commanded not to cause a blemish in the holy offerings in order to eat them, for he who causes a blemish in the holy offerings by his own choice, also the prohibition of work and shearing in the holy offerings, for even the broken tablets are holy.

### **The sum** of the matter is that the service is the offering, however, the internal offering is the man. And likewise, his soul is called after his death to the altar above, and Michael is the High Priest. And the matter is the secret that "in the image of God was man made." Therefore, the warning came to be careful in his life regarding the damage to souls, not to kill a man except after thorough inquiry and investigation. And then it is "given into the hands of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the witness and He is the judge," for the Lord, may He be blessed, is a true witness and a true judge. So must the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <gloss>high court</gloss> be; just as they are true judges, so must they be true witnesses. I mean to say that they must have the clarification of the truth of the witnesses in complete clarity, that is, the inquiry and investigation. And then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven. "And precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death." <note>Psalm 116:15</note>

### **And since** "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death," for Israel are holy from the side of their souls, which after their death the souls cleave above, therefore the commandment came, "You shall not cut yourselves, you shall not make a bald spot," etc., "for you are children to the Lord your God." <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note> This is not so for the nations; the cutting and the bald spot are from their customs, for so it is appropriate since in their death they go to perdition and they have no portion neither in this world nor in the world to come. This is not so for us, the children of the living God. And when one departs from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, or rather, we have a permanent dwelling above with our Father in Heaven, therefore it is forbidden to increase in mourning and to do these acts.

### **Let us return** to the matter, for the man who serves is himself the offering, as it is written, "When a man among you offers." And there is more in this, a secret. For the sparks that were scattered, even below, the man, that is, in the secret of the reincarnation, "Man and beast You shall save, O Lord." <note>Psalm 36:7</note> Therefore, even in the eating of ordinary food, the meat of desire, we were commanded in the slaughtering and with great care without a nick, for then it is a carcass, and then it becomes a carcass in Israel. For who knows what reincarnation is in it? "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself," choose for him a beautiful death, that is, slaughtering without a nick. And if the beast died of itself, or it spread and the power of impurity took hold of it. But when he slaughters it properly, and there is in the beast, its sacrifice, and like a pure bird, a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **And he who eats** a limb from a living creature is like one who eats from the flesh of a person when there is a reincarnation of a soul there. And this is the secret, "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." <note>Deuteronomy 12:23</note> And likewise the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of the pure beast, animal, and bird, all point to the spark that is spread in them, whether it is from the side of impurity or from the side of holiness. And I have elaborated on this in the portion of <term>Shemini</term> <gloss>Eighth</gloss>. And Israel, when they conduct themselves in holiness, it is written about them, "And they shall make Me a sanctuary and I will dwell in their midst," <note>Exodus 25:8</note> for they themselves are the tabernacle. For here the man is like three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies, the heart corresponds to the Holy, and then from the belly and below corresponds to the courtyard of the Holy, as I have elaborated in the portion of <term>Terumah</term> <gloss>Heave-offering</gloss>. And when he eats foods that are from the side of holiness, then they are like an offering offered upon the altar. And regarding this, our Sages of blessed memory said, "Now the table of a man atones," as I have elaborated in its place.

### **And the matter** of the commandments of the festivals and their offerings, I have written the matters of each one in its special place. And the commandment came to rejoice on the festivals and to ascend for the festival, "And three times a year shall every male of yours appear." <note>Exodus 23:17</note> And it does not say "to see," but rather, in the way that he comes to see, so he comes to be seen. Therefore, if he wishes to be seen in the Temple, where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. For without this, it is forbidden to appear in the hall of the wicked, and how will he wish to appear before Him, may He be blessed? And he brings a burnt offering of appearance, and then he himself is an offering through the offering that he offers. And it said, "Three times a year he shall appear," Isaac, who lived, is a perfect burnt offering.

### On the shame felt from undeserved praise.
## DIAL. XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you condemn again, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy person.

<note>A large, decorative initial letter L marks the beginning of the response from Reason.</note>

*Reason.* You are accused of having praised an unworthy person. That which is evil often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they are themselves, imagine others to be the same. Hence, they are even more prone to praise; and although I admit that praising an unworthy person is a bad thing, it is nevertheless much worse to disparage one who is undeserving.

*Sorrow.* I have praised an unworthy person.

*Reason.* If you did it knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is less of an evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another, but to deceive is the crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another turns into my own infamy.

*Reason.* On the contrary, it is your own fault or your own ignorance. For just as there is no praise to be gained from another, so there is no infamy.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly that I have praised an unworthy person.

*Reason.* See to it, therefore, that you do not grieve over this very thing often. Beware of rushing rashly into praising and disparaging. How does nothing prevent them from being stars, even if they are not similar, just as nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same lot as the others, even if they do not have a similar face? Do you not see how contrary the elements are to one another? There are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, that one which returns to its place in the thirtieth year is very similar to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not provide its work according to one form, but prides itself on variety. It made some things more sluggish, others swifter than the rest. It made some stronger, others more temperate, and some it led out from the crowd so that they might proceed individually and conspicuously, while others it sent into a flock. He is ignorant of the power of nature who does not think it is permitted to do anything except what it does most often. It does not show comets frequently; it assigns them another place, other times, and motions unlike the others. It wished to honor the magnitude of its work through these, whose appearance is too beautiful to be thought accidental, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more burning than the rest. Indeed, their appearance has something remarkable and singular, not cast and tightened into a narrow space, but sent forth more freely, and embracing the region of many stars. <meta>continues from previous page</meta> and other things with it. The one being purged must not hasten to consume many or poor-quality foods, lest nature attract them while they are undigested. If something of that sort is necessary, it must be in very small amounts, spaced out so that it is gradual, and what enters the body must be well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for blood. As for evacuation specific to a humor that has increased in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is other than phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive causes fainting in most cases. If the cessation of diarrhea was caused by a habit, it is a sign that the evacuation should be repeated, as the body is accustomed to it, such as in the case of one whose cessation of nosebleeds or sneezing caused blockages; for returning to that habit removes them. Know that the remainder of the material that needs to be purged is less susceptible to being completely removed, and pushing it to the point where strength fails is wrong. Often, nature dissolves that remainder itself. As long as the humor is of the type that is appropriate and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess. Sometimes you may need to purge until fainting occurs. Whoever has strong power and a large amount of bad humors should be purged little by little. Likewise, if the material is highly matured or strongly mixed with blood and cannot be purged all at once, this is the case in sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that diarrhea draws from above and clears from below, so it is consistent with the familiar attraction. It is also consistent after the materials have settled; if the materials are from below, it draws them to it by opposition and clears them from where they are, and this is by the action of attraction and vice versa. The state of phlebotomy varies according to the places from which blood is taken, as you have learned. The people least in need of evacuation are those with good digestion, and those in hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say it is recommended for one who wishes to be purged to eat or space out their food, and the first amount of the dose they test in a day should be in portions, and they should make them different foods and different drinks. For the stomach is affected by this state, such that it desires to push what is in it upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, but rather one food after another, the stomach becomes satisfied with it, relaxes, and grips it tightly, especially if it is small in quantity. As for those with a naturally loose constitution, none of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not occur to one who has a good regimen; they need what is lighter than that. Perhaps exercise, massage, and cupping will suffice for them. Then, if their body is filled with the most abundant filling of the best humors, meaning blood, then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, not diarrhea. If necessity dictates phlebotomy or evacuation, such as in the autumn, and one is inclined toward vomiting, it is furthered by phlebotomy. This is from the advice of Hippocrates and the books that follow it, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood, and if the humors are equal, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy might increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In summary, if the humors are equal, prioritize phlebotomy; if they are not equal, purge the excess first until they are equal, then perform phlebotomy. Whoever prioritizes medicine over phlebotomy should have prioritized phlebotomy, even if only a little. Whoever was recently bled and needed to be purged, and drank medicine, it was stopped for him. Often, drinking the medicine when phlebotomy was required caused fainting and agitation. If it does not subside with sedatives, then phlebotomy should have been prioritized. There is no evacuation needed for excessive fullness that is not called for by the severity of the illness and the fullness according to quality and quantity. Often, good regimen prevents the need for phlebotomy at the time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but an obstacle opposes it, so the only trick for it is fasting, sleep, and correcting the bad temperament by way of fullness. Some evacuation is by way of precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other things at a known time, especially in the spring. So it is necessary to take precautions before its time and perform the specific evacuation, whether it be phlebotomy or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines is a form of evacuation, such as what is done with those suffering from dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous to the humor being purged in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> <gloss>a purgative resin</gloss> when you need to purge yellow bile. It is necessary then to mix with it what opposes it in quality and agrees with it in diarrhea, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <gloss>a dried fruit used as a laxative</gloss>. Correcting the bad temperament if it occurs afterward in those with visceral tumors weakens their diarrhea. If you are forced to do that, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for the purgative and <term>cassia fistula</term> <gloss>purging cassia</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a constitution that easily responds to vomiting, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring when it is time, for that relieves the body of fatigue." Know that the one who is accustomed to a loose constitution or is not accustomed to vomiting should avoid it when there is no need. It is necessary to prepare before diarrhea by softening the humor one wishes to purge and widening the passages at that time, for that relieves the body of fatigue. Know that the one who is accustomed to a loose constitution or is not accustomed to vomiting, before using strong medicine, should use one of the regimens that reduce and purge. Diarrhea with emaciation of the abdomen is difficult and tiring, and the purging medicine might return as a laxative if the stomach is strong, or if it was drunk on an empty stomach, or if the drinker has a loose constitution, or because of the medicine, or if the medicine was heavier in substance than what descends quickly. The purgative might remain, causing pain due to the weakness of the stomach, or extreme heaviness, or because the medicine distressed it, or because the person had indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge undigested matter, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it in the body, so it takes over the body and attracts other humors to it, and that humor increases in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting in most cases, such as yellow bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a state like milk and stars <note>likely a reference to specific humoral textures</note>, and its diarrhea is more correct in itself. Whoever has a humor that is descending, such as those with intestinal slippage, the tightening of the intestines hinders the purgative medicine. What is composed of medicines that are strongly different in the time of diarrhea causes the diarrhea to be agitated, and the first purges the second before the second purges, and perhaps the first purges the second itself. Whoever is exposed to diarrhea and his body is not cleansed of it must have medicine, and colic and distress befall him, and what is purged is purged with great difficulty. In summary, the medicine that purges the superfluities does not cause agitation. If it is taken with agitation, it either purges what is not a superfluity, or if the purged humor changes by vomiting or diarrhea to another humor, it indicates the body is cleansed of the humor intended to be purged.

What, therefore, is the manner in which God foreknows these uncertain future events? For if He deems them to be avoidable future events, and it is not possible for them to happen, He is deceived; and to think this is not only wicked, but even to utter it. But if He discerns that they will be future events in such a way that He knows they can either happen or not happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this that grasps nothing certain and nothing stable? Or how does this differ from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias, who said, "Whatever I shall say will either be or not be"? Why, then, should divine prudence differ from human opinion if it judges uncertain things just as men do, whose outcome is uncertain? # Question

The third article. Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

It is proceeded thus: that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition. Because those things which are prior according to nature are posterior and less known according to us, but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior regarding us, and simple things are posterior. But universals are prior; therefore, they are known later regarding us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition, and the less universal is a part of the definition: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "human," and universals are known later regarding us. Furthermore, effects occur by chance and by principles. But universals are known later regarding us. But if it is that, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*, one must proceed from universals to singulars. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive [cognition]. And because sense is of singulars, and intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior regarding us than the cognition of universals. Second, one must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known in act and in a certain way in potency. As the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: things are first manifest and certain to us in a more confused way. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, however, both the whole in which parts are contained in potency and the integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole, however, is to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know the animal in which there is rational or irrational, which is to know a human or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and to know "human." And to fall into reason if I compare whatever is more or less, as sense exits from potency into act, so does the intellect; this is the order

<column-break/>

of cognition that appears in the sense. For more is known in the sense and divided more, and when less is known, it is more remote through <unclear>the being of a body</unclear>, and <unclear>the being of a body</unclear> and "animal"; and more is known as "animal" and <unclear>the being of a body</unclear> and <unclear>the good</unclear> and prior <unclear>good</unclear> and <unclear>sort</unclear>. Or it pleases and is evident that a child from the beginning distinguishes "good" and "not good" first; and in children from the beginning they call all men "fathers." Later, however, he terminates each one as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: for it is manifest that he who knows something indistinctly still knows it in potency, or he knows <unclear>the fiction</unclear> and the principle, and thus he knows <unclear>the genus</unclear> and is able to know <unclear>the species</unclear>. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is intermediate between potency and act. And that the cognition of singulars is prior regarding us, and the cognition of the universal is [posterior to] sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If both sense and intellect are considered, the cognition of the less [universal] and common is prior. To the first, it must be said that it can be considered in a twofold way. One way is that it is considered according to the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true are the same, it has a relationship to many things. It arrives at the abstraction of the intellect, and this is the end, while the truth is posterior. In the first book of *De Anima*, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but <unclear>Plato</unclear> posited universals as substances; and in this consideration, it is true, more because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal subsisting things which are called ideas. In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifest in the generation of a human and an animal. For an animal is generated before a human, as the Philosopher says in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. Another is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature to that which is perfect, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect; and in this way, the less universal is prior in nature, for nature's intention does not stop at the generation of an animal, but it intends to generate a human. To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole which is made more universal, not only "human" and "horse," as it can be, and the less universal is contained in the future, not only the more universal but also others, as "human" is not only "animal" but "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition than "human." If "human" is prior in our cognition, then "animal" is so through its reason. To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is <unclear>a house</unclear>. In another way, when it is a part of this whole, and stones, it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house first in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the definition to be considered absolutely is prior to us and the defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified by those things. But rather, they are the parts.

When the Lion awoke the next morning, the judge entered with a group of prominent companions, carrying the document containing Dimna’s excuses. The Lion took the document and ordered them to depart.

He then sent for his mother and read the document to her. It distressed her, and she said, "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion replied, "I will not be angry, so say whatever you wish."

She said, "I do not see that you distinguish between what harms you and what benefits you. I believe that by delaying your decision regarding Dimna, you will incite a situation against yourself that you will be unable to withstand or overcome."

She then stood up and left in anger. The next day, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing.

The judge said to him, "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life once the accusation has settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt. This will free your neck from the consequences in the afterlife, and a good reputation may return to you for two reasons: first, your ability to provide excuses and fabricate justifications that defend yourself; and second, your voluntary confession of guilt, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: death in a manner that is honorable is better than life in a manner that is shameful."

Dimna answered him, saying, "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. You know that suspicion does not replace the truth in any way. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I have knowledge of myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My situation has only appeared ugly to you, if that is indeed the case, because you suspected that I strove..."

So one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the money minus one-eighth of a bequest. One-eighth of the money minus one-eighth of a bequest, together with the bequest, equals a sister's portion. That is one-eighth of the money and seven-eighths of a bequest. The whole money equals three-eighths of the money and three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. Subtract three-eighths of the money from the money, and there remains five-eighths of the money, which equals three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. The whole money equals five bequests and four-fifths of a bequest. The money is twenty-nine, the bequest is five, and the portion is eight.

In another method of bequests: a man died and left four sons, and he bequeathed to a man the equivalent of one of his sons' portions, and to another a quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the bequest is only from a third.

3223. There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things that are in him. The things that are there, even though they do not appear to be of that light, still are; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus, unless they have some form from the light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which in the natural man contribute so much that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. The light of heaven, however, is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and ascribes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily things, he has only a perception of such things as belong to the light of the world, and not of such things as belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the entire heaven is in that light. This light—namely, the light of heaven—is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Those things that form one ray in the light of the world form myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven there is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no perception at all, for the things that belong to the light of the world have life from that source. Between these lights, or between those things that are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual man—that is, when the former serves the latter. And the things that then exist in the light of the world are representative of such things as are in the light of heaven.

# We have set the distance

from noon because the adjustment for the birth <note>referring to the astronomical new moon or conjunction</note> is easier than working with horizons and the longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem, which is fourteen hours and some fraction. Therefore, the Jewish practice of using temporal hours <note>hours of varying length based on the division of daylight</note> is not consistent unless the conjunction for the beginning of Tishrei <note>the first month of the Jewish civil year</note> happens to coincide with the autumnal equinox. It never coincides with it; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have explained previously. Once we have derived the time of the conjunction using the calculation that the Jews provided in the table we analyzed according to their view, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the beginning of the year and the understanding of its nature regarding deficiency, equilibrium, and fullness. We have already gained knowledge of whether it is a common or a leap year. We then search in the table of limits for a duration of days of the week whose boundaries encompass the time at which the conjunction occurred for us, in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, and in the section for common years if it is a common year. Once we find it, we discover alongside it the beginning of the year in terms of the days of the week and its nature. When we know the beginning of the year and its nature, and we combine that nature with the common or leap year status, we know from that the passage of the beginning of the next year.

Entering into meditative equipoise, the state in which one does not provide an opportunity for afflictions to arise in the mental continuum of others through the power of previous aspirations is called the meditative equipoise of being without afflictions. Regarding the question, "What is the knowledge of aspiration?", it refers to the phenomena included within the scope of what is to be known from among the phenomena of the three times and the three realms. Because one has made an aspiration to know any phenomenon whatsoever, whether mundane or supramundane, the knowledge that immediately realizes that phenomenon as a result of that aspiration is called knowledge preceded by aspiration, or "aspirational knowledge."

Regarding the question, "What are the four purities?", they are as follows: The state in which all the latent predispositions <note>original: "gnas ngan len" (dausthulya), the subtle seeds of afflictions</note> of the afflictions of all sentient beings are completely removed from their basis, the ability to assume one's own body as one wishes, and having mastery over abiding and passing away, is the purity of the basis. Having mastery over emanations, over the categories of transformation, and over all objects of focus is the purity of the object of focus. Being free from all latent predispositions of the mind, such that virtue increases in the mind in all aspects, is the purity of the mind. Being free from all latent predispositions on the side of ignorance, such that knowledge is unobstructed and has mastery over all that is to be known, is the purity of primordial wisdom.

Regarding the question, "What are the ten masteries?", they are as follows: Remaining for as long as one wishes is mastery over life. Abiding in meditative concentration, immeasurable states, liberations, and so forth, in whatever way one wishes to abide, is mastery over the mind. The immediate attainment of all necessities, such as food, simply by conceptualizing them, exactly as one wishes, is mastery over necessities. Having mastery over all actions that lead to rebirth, exactly as one wishes,

To transform according to one's wishes is mastery over action. In all places of birth, to be born wherever and however one wishes is mastery over birth. Whatever things one aspires to, that they are accomplished accordingly is mastery over aspiration. All of one's prayers being fulfilled exactly as desired is mastery over prayer. All purposes of miraculous power being accomplished exactly as desired is mastery over miraculous power. Those who wish to know profound objects of knowledge, to know them quickly is mastery over pristine wisdom. To obtain collections of names, collections of phrases, and collections of syllables exactly as desired, and to be skilled in the perfect arrangement of all phenomena, is mastery over the Dharma.

Regarding the question, "What are the three non-protections of the Tathagata?" the three non-protections are easily understood from the text itself. The three foundations of mindfulness, free from attachment and aversion, are easily understood. The nature of having no forgetfulness means that whenever and however the Tathagata works for the benefit of sentient beings, he accomplishes it accordingly; this is the nature of having no forgetfulness. Everyone knows that although it appears to have a complexion, it is not like the complexion of our own bodies. # The Explanation of the Noble Sutra of the Four Dharmas

Homage to <term>Manjushri Kumara-bhuta</term> <gloss>the youthful Manjushri</gloss>.

Why was this sutra, which states, "A bodhisattva, a great being, should not abandon these four dharmas even for the sake of their life as long as they live," composed? It was composed to correctly instruct those who are confused about the methods for attaining unsurpassed enlightenment, having entered the Great Vehicle; to correctly guide those who are heedless; to correctly encourage those who are discouraged; and to bring great joy to those who have correctly entered the path.

The number "four" is mentioned to avoid vastness, so that those who do not wish to listen to such things may be avoided. Mentioning the number also allows for easy recollection. Regarding the patience and gentleness that appear later, they are not distinct because they serve the same purpose.

Although there are many categories for those who have entered the Great Vehicle, two names are mentioned for three reasons: through aspiration, through application, and through realization. What is meant by aspiration? One is a "bodhisattva" because one aspires to profound objects of knowledge. One is a "great being" because one aspires to great power. What is meant by application? It is because one strives for unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment for oneself, and because one strives to fully protect all sentient beings from suffering. What is meant by realization? It is because enlightenment is realized through two powers. What are the two? They are the power of intellect and the power of diligence. <margin>Poison exists even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? All are forced to admit this. If this is true, then I ask you now: should poison not be separated from the good and useful? And should the good be accepted and the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I ask you to explain to me: how is this separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted to admit that poison lies hidden there, and you are asked where it eventually goes, you then bring forth I know not what about "corrections" that supposedly extract and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is ventilated.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or after Diagridium. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it was at first? And yet you boast in the meantime that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it gone?
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test this, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know this not sluggishly. Thus you also correct Turbith, and call it Diaturbith. Such are your corrections, which would befit rustics and should be given to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see whether you will not feel the poison.
<margin>What "to correct" means for a physician.</margin>
*To correct is to take what is corrected.* Whoever is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who has been punished lasts. Such are these corrections too; it is up to them, not up to you. Now, in this case, the physician must consider nothing more than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without any harm. The same must be understood equally regarding all other things, namely, that a similar separation is necessary. That not yet being done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless perhaps it happens that nature supplies your place, or the greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will remain.

Now, therefore, if that true foundation is necessary which removes the poison, how does Alchemy perform this? For it must be done in such a way that, if Mars <note>alchemical symbol for iron</note> is in the Sun <note>alchemical symbol for gold</note>, Mars must be removed; and if Saturn <note>alchemical symbol for lead</note> is found in Venus <note>alchemical symbol for copper</note>, it must be separated from it. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist in them. But those bodies which are contrary, it is necessary that some of them be entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety may be lifted, and the evil which you seek may be taken away from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so much less useful is medicine that does not pass through fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into another generation, which ought to conduce to and assist man. And should this not deservedly be considered the proper foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to apply poisons, but true secrets.
